slides.title: Sorting Experts by Consistent Criteria
bullets: Segmentation sorts territory experts into meaningful tiers
Based on defined, consistent criteria, not who is easiest to reach
Lets engagement effort be allocated deliberately

slides.title: What Segmentation Actually Measures
bullets: Scientific influence: publications, trial leadership, guidelines, congresses
Digital influence: reach, engagement quality, community trust
Strategic relevance: fit with current therapeutic priorities
Relationship stage: established, early, or not yet engaged

slides.title: The Three-Tier Model
bullets: Tier 1: broadest, most established influence, shapes national practice
Tier 1 engagement often involves senior Medical Affairs leadership
Tier 2: respected regional or national experts needing local context
Tier 3: emerging experts and clinical champions with local influence

slides.title: What Each Tier Actually Needs
bullets: Tier 1: advisory boards, trial-design input, sustained partnership
Tier 2: help translating global evidence into local guideline context
Tier 3: relationship-building and disease-state education

slides.title: Consistency Protects Scarce Time and Trust
bullets: Explicit criteria applied consistently, not decided meeting by meeting
Reserves scarce senior time for the experts who truly warrant it
Creates a defensible, compliance-friendly rationale for engagement

slides.title: Segmentation Needs Field Input
bullets: Not a one-time exercise handed down from headquarters
Territory-level judgment keeps the model accurate over time
Sets up the next lesson on advanced KOL mapping

takeaway.title: Segmentation allocates engagement effort deliberately, using consistent criteria
bullets: Scientific influence, digital influence, strategic relevance and relationship stage all count
The three-tier model matches engagement intensity to each tier's real needs
Field-level judgment keeps segmentation accurate, not headquarters alone
